title: The Burned-over District
description: Revival fire in western New York and why so many movements started there

concepts.title: A Region on Fire
concepts.contentHtml:
In August 1801 a camp meeting at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, drew a crowd nobody counted. Guesses ran as high as 20,000, and observers described people falling, weeping and jerking under conviction of sin. It belonged to the Second Great Awakening, the name historians give to a long wave of Protestant revivals in the United States, usually dated from about 1790 to the 1840s. The wave had no single center. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist farmer-preachers carried this style of religion across the new republic, and their churches grew fastest.

In western and central New York the wave struck with unusual force in the 1820s and 1830s. The region was filling quickly, largely with migrants from New England. The Erie Canal, opened in 1825 to link the Hudson River with Lake Erie, turned farm villages into market towns almost overnight, and Rochester grew from about 1,500 people in 1820 to about 9,000 in 1830.1 New towns had new churches, few settled ministers, and a population used to arguing about salvation.

The district's name comes from the era's most famous revivalist. In memoirs published in 1876, after his death, Charles Grandison Finney recalled finding a region that "in the western phrase, would be called, a 'burnt district'", meaning ground where earlier, in his view spurious, excitements had left people hardened, like a forest with nothing left to burn. Contemporaries rarely used the label. It became standard after the historian Whitney R. Cross titled his 1950 study The Burned-over District, and it now covers a band of western and central New York from Lake Erie east past the Finger Lakes to Oneida County.

concepts.title: Charles Finney and the New Measures
concepts.contentHtml:
Finney (1792 to 1875) was born in Connecticut and grew up in upstate New York. He was training as a lawyer in Adams, Jefferson County, when he underwent a conversion in October 1821, and he later said he now had "a retainer from the Lord Jesus Christ to plead his cause." He was ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1824, though he later admitted he had barely read the Westminster Confession he affirmed, and he came to reject its teaching that sinners cannot turn to God by their own choice. From 1825 he led revivals in Oneida County towns such as Western, Rome and Utica.

Critics called his methods the New Measures. They treated revival as something a minister could organize. He held protracted meetings that ran nightly for days or weeks. He set an "anxious bench" at the front, where people struggling over their souls sat to be prayed for in public. He prayed for sinners by name, and he let women pray aloud in mixed gatherings. In his Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) he wrote that a revival "is not a miracle, or dependent on a miracle, in any sense." It was the result of the right use of means, as a harvest follows planting.

Older evangelicals, led by Lyman Beecher and Asahel Nettleton, confronted Finney's camp at New Lebanon, New York, in July 1827, and the meeting ended without agreement. His best-known campaign came in Rochester from September 1830 into 1831, when hundreds joined the town's churches. He later preached in New York City, condemned slavery from the pulpit and refused communion to slaveholders, and in 1835 moved to Oberlin College in Ohio, which he served as president from 1851 to 1866.

concepts.title: Why There? A Crowded Field and Its Explanations
concepts.contentHtml:
The district bred or sheltered a long run of movements. From the late 1780s the preacher called the Public Universal Friend, formerly Jemima Wilkinson, who claimed no gender, settled followers near Seneca Lake. In 1830 Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon at Palmyra, a text he said he had translated from golden plates an angel had shown him, and that April he organized a church whose largest heir, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, now reports more than 17 million members.1 Millerism drew heavy support here, the Fox sisters' rappings at Hydesville in 1848 launched Spiritualism, and the Oneida Community settled near Oneida that year. Reform crusades flourished too, from Antimasonry and temperance to abolition and the 1848 women's rights convention at Seneca Falls.

Cross explained the pattern through the people rather than the frontier. In his account the zeal peaked after the pioneer stage had passed, and it came from transplanted New Englanders, many from Vermont and western Massachusetts, with high literacy and an intense Puritan-descended piety. Paul Johnson's A Shopkeeper's Millennium (1978) read the Rochester revival as a response by employers to the breakdown of the household workshop, when masters no longer lived with their workmen. Converts then pressed temperance and discipline on workers. Mary Ryan's Cradle of the Middle Class (1981), on Oneida County, showed that women usually converted first and drew husbands and children after them.

Critics charge Johnson with reducing religious experience to class interest. A statistical study by Linda Pritchard (1984) found the district's religiosity roughly typical of New York, the Ohio Valley and the nation, which implies that its new movements set it apart rather than unusual everyday piety.

title: The Shakers
description: Ann Lee's celibate Believers, their dances, songs and chairs, and the last village

concepts.title: Mother Ann Lee and the Shaking Quakers
concepts.contentHtml:
The Shakers' formal name is the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing. They began in northwest England, where in 1747 a small group around James and Jane Wardley broke from the Quakers. Their meetings in Bolton and Manchester were loud and physical: worshippers trembled, shouted, sang and whirled under what they felt as the power of the spirit, which earned them the mocking name "Shaking Quakers."

Ann Lee (1736 to 1784), an illiterate blacksmith's daughter from Manchester who had worked in a cotton mill, joined the group in 1758. In 1761 she married Abraham Standerin, also a blacksmith; all four of her children died in infancy, losses many biographers connect with her later conviction that sexual desire lay at the root of human sin. Jailed for disrupting Sabbath worship, she reported a revelation that Adam and Eve's fall had been a sexual act, and that the path to holiness lay in confessing sins and renouncing sex. Followers began to call her Mother Ann.

In 1774 Lee and eight followers sailed for New York on the Mariah, arriving that August, and by the late 1770s they had settled at Niskayuna, later Watervliet, near Albany. From 1781 to 1783 Lee toured Massachusetts and Connecticut, where mobs beat Shakers, suspicious of their celibacy, their English origins in wartime and their refusal to bear arms. She died at Watervliet in September 1784, aged 48. Many Believers came to see her as the female embodiment of the Christ spirit, the "second appearing" of their name. Most of her recorded sayings come from Testimonies gathered from followers and printed in 1816, so scholars read them as remembered tradition, not transcripts.

concepts.title: Celibate Families and Shared Authority
concepts.contentHtml:
After Lee's death, Joseph Meacham, a former Baptist preacher, and Lucy Wright organized the converts into self-contained communal villages under what they called "gospel order." Members signed a covenant and gave their property to the community, and by the 1790s villages had been "gathered" at New Lebanon (later Mount Lebanon), Watervliet and across New England. Missions after 1805 added villages in Ohio, Kentucky and Indiana. Estimates of peak membership, reached around the 1840s, run from about 4,000 to 6,000 Believers in roughly 18 major communities from Maine to Kentucky.

Each village was divided into "families," each living in a large dwelling house with separate doors and staircases for men and women. Celibacy was absolute, so the Society grew only by conversion and by taking in children, often orphans or the children of converts; many left when they came of age. Leadership was paired by sex from top to bottom. The central Ministry at New Lebanon had two elders and two eldresses, and every family had its own elders and eldresses, deacons and deaconesses. Lucy Wright led the whole Society from 1796 to 1821.

That parallel structure gave women more formal authority than almost any other American institution of the time, and Shaker theology came to speak of a God who was both Father and Mother. The equality had limits. Work followed conventional lines, with sisters mostly in kitchens, laundries and sewing rooms and brothers in fields and shops, and women supervised women while men supervised men. The Society also crossed racial lines more than most churches: Rebecca Cox Jackson, a free Black preacher who joined at Watervliet, founded a small, largely Black Shaker family in Philadelphia in the late 1850s.

concepts.title: Gifts: Dance, Song, Furniture and the Last Village
concepts.contentHtml:
Shaker worship moved from spontaneous shaking and whirling to drilled communal dance, with lines of brothers and sisters shuffling, turning and marching in set patterns. From 1837 until about 1850 came the Era of Manifestations, or "Mother's Work," when members, many of them young, fell into trances and delivered messages, songs and "gifts" said to come from Mother Ann and other spirits. Its legacy includes a flood of songs and "gift drawings" such as Hannah Cohoon's Tree of Life (1854). The best-known Shaker song, "Simple Gifts" ("'Tis the gift to be simple"), is a dance song dated to 1848 and credited to Elder Joseph Brackett of the Maine Shakers. It reached a wide public only when Aaron Copland used it in his ballet Appalachian Spring (1944).

Plainness also shaped Shaker workmanship. Their furniture avoided carving, inlay and veneer as vanity and relied on proportion: ladder-back chairs, built-in cupboards, peg rails for hanging chairs out of the way, and bentwood oval boxes. Mount Lebanon was selling chairs commercially by the 1860s. Shakers were also among the first to sell garden seeds in small paper packets. Popular claims that they invented the flat broom or the circular saw rest on community tradition rather than firm evidence.

Membership fell steadily after the Civil War. In 1957 the leading eldresses, based at Canterbury, New Hampshire, voted to close the covenant to new members, but Sabbathday Lake, in New Gloucester, Maine, went on quietly admitting a few converts. Canterbury's last Shaker died in 1992. When Sister Frances Carr died in 2017, two Believers remained, Brother Arnold Hadd and Sister June Carpenter; a newcomer began living with them in 2025.

title: The Oneida Community
description: John Humphrey Noyes, perfectionism, complex marriage and a silverware company

concepts.title: John Humphrey Noyes and the Doctrine of Perfection
concepts.contentHtml:
John Humphrey Noyes (1811 to 1886) was born in Brattleboro, Vermont, into a well-off family; his father served a term in Congress. After graduating from Dartmouth he was converted in a revival in 1831, in the style Finney had made famous, and went on to study for the ministry at Andover and Yale. At New Haven he joined the radical edge of perfectionism, the belief that Christians could become entirely free of sin in this life.

Noyes pushed the idea further than most. He argued that the Second Coming of Christ had already happened, in 70 CE, the year Roman forces destroyed the Jerusalem Temple, so the promised kingdom could be lived now rather than awaited. In 1834 he declared himself free from sin, and his license to preach was withdrawn. He is said to have replied that he had taken away their license to sin and they kept on sinning, so though they had taken away his license to preach, he would keep on preaching.

Back in Putney, Vermont, he gathered a Bible school from about 1836 that became a small communal group practicing what he called "Bible communism": shared property and, from the mid-1840s, shared sexual partners. Noyes cited Jesus's saying that in the resurrection people "neither marry, nor are given in marriage" (Matthew 22:30). Exclusive marriage, like private property, was to him a selfish form of ownership the kingdom had abolished. Indicted for adultery in 1847, he left Vermont, and in 1848 his followers regrouped on land at Oneida, New York. The Oneida Community grew to about 300 members, with a smaller branch at Wallingford, Connecticut.

concepts.title: Complex Marriage, Criticism and Stirpiculture
concepts.contentHtml:
At Oneida every adult man was considered married to every adult woman, a system Noyes called complex marriage. Exclusive romantic attachment, "special love," was criticized as selfish, and so was too strong a bond between parents and their own children, who lived in a separate children's house from early childhood. Sexual encounters were supposed to be voluntary and were often arranged through an intermediary, usually an older woman. For birth control, men were expected to practice what Noyes called male continence, a form of coitus reservatus; the community recorded about a dozen unplanned births among some 200 adults between 1848 and 1868.

The system had a hierarchy. Under the principle of "ascending fellowship," members were urged to seek relations with those judged more spiritually advanced, which in practice meant older members and above all Noyes. Adolescents were introduced to sex by older members; diaries and later memoirs show that girls were usually initiated soon after puberty, often by Noyes himself. Many historians now describe this as the sexual exploitation of minors. Discipline came through mutual criticism, sessions in which a member sat silent while a committee, or the whole community, listed his or her faults.

In 1869 Noyes launched stirpiculture, from Latin stirps, "stock" or "root": a program of planned human breeding. A committee under his strong influence approved or proposed couples judged spiritually and physically fit. By the commonly cited count, 53 women and 38 men took part and 58 children were born before the program ended in 1879, at least nine of them fathered by Noyes. It began more than a decade before Francis Galton coined the word "eugenics" in 1883.

concepts.title: Breakup and the Silverware
concepts.contentHtml:
Oneida was a business success. Its most profitable product was a steel animal trap designed by member Sewell Newhouse and sold widely to trappers. The community also made traveling bags, silk thread and canned fruit, and by the 1870s it employed outside workers. Members lived together in the Mansion House, a large brick dwelling built in stages from the 1860s that still stands as a museum.

By the late 1870s the community was under strain. Younger members, some educated at Yale, questioned Noyes's religious authority. His attempt to hand leadership to his son Theodore, an agnostic, failed. Clergy in the region, led by John W. Mears of Hamilton College, campaigned against the community. In June 1879, warned that a warrant for his arrest on statutory rape charges was imminent, Noyes fled to Canada. That August, on his advice, the community gave up complex marriage, and many members married conventionally.

On January 1, 1881, the community reorganized as a joint-stock company, Oneida Community, Limited, with members receiving shares in place of common property. Noyes died at Niagara Falls, Ontario, in 1886. The community had begun making spoons in 1877, and from 1899 silver-plated flatware sold as "Community Plate" became the company's main line. Pierrepont Noyes, one of the stirpiculture children and a son of John Humphrey Noyes, led the business in the early twentieth century and promoted the nearby company town of Sherrill. Oneida became one of the best-known American tableware brands, then ended US manufacturing in 2005 and went through bankruptcy in 2006; the brand has since passed to other owners.

title: Colonies of Heaven and Reason
description: The Harmony Society, Owen's New Harmony, Brook Farm and the Amana Colonies

concepts.title: The Harmony Society: Waiting for the Millennium
concepts.contentHtml:
Johann Georg Rapp (1757 to 1847), a weaver and lay preacher from Iptingen in Württemberg, led Pietist separatists who broke with the Lutheran state church in the 1780s. Under pressure from church and state authorities, Rapp went to America in 1803, and several hundred followers came after him in 1804. On February 15, 1805, about 400 members formally organized the Harmony Society at Harmony, in Butler County, Pennsylvania, pooling their property.

The Harmonists, or Rappites, expected Christ to return within their lifetimes. Around 1807 they adopted celibacy, to make themselves pure for the coming millennium; married couples were not separated by divorce but lived as brother and sister. The Society grew rich through farming, wool and cotton mills, and wine and whiskey. In 1814 it sold Harmony and moved to the Wabash River in Indiana, then in 1824 and 1825 to a third town, Economy, on the Ohio River below Pittsburgh.

Celibacy meant the Society would dwindle unless it recruited. In 1832 a newcomer calling himself "Count de Leon," Bernhard Müller, claimed prophetic authority and split the community: about 250 of some 750 members left with him. The remaining Harmonists invested shrewdly in railroads, oil and other industries, and grew richer as they grew fewer. By 1905 only a handful survived, and the Society was dissolved with assets of over a million dollars. Old Economy Village, in present-day Ambridge, Pennsylvania, preserves its buildings. The pattern of a celibate community prospering as it aged, and dying out with money in the bank, would repeat among the Shakers.

concepts.title: New Harmony: Robert Owen's Secular Utopia
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1825 the Harmonists sold their Indiana town to Robert Owen (1771 to 1858), a Welsh-born cotton manufacturer famous for his model mill village at New Lanark in Scotland, where he had limited child labor and opened schools. Sources give the price as either $125,000 or $150,000. Owen held that character is formed by circumstances rather than chosen, so a rationally designed environment would produce rational, cooperative people. He set out his plan in two addresses in the chamber of the US House of Representatives in February and March 1825.

New Harmony drew some 700 to 800 settlers within months, many of them short of the farming and craft skills the town needed. In January 1826 a keelboat, the Philanthropist, nicknamed the "Boatload of Knowledge," brought the geologist William Maclure, the naturalist Thomas Say, the artist Charles-Alexandre Lesueur and a group of educators. On July 4, 1826, Owen issued a "Declaration of Mental Independence" denouncing a trinity of evils: private property, irrational systems of religion, and marriage founded on property.

The community split into rival societies within a year, and Owen left in June 1827 after spending much of his fortune. The usual explanations are quarrels over who worked and who did not, a shortage of skilled labor, and Owen's open hostility to religion, which alienated many of the farming families he hoped to attract. Yet the town left a scientific and educational legacy. Owen's son Robert Dale Owen, as a congressman, introduced the 1846 bill that created the Smithsonian Institution, and another son, David Dale Owen, led early federal geological surveys from New Harmony. In 1854 the elder Owen, long a critic of religion, embraced Spiritualism.

concepts.title: Brook Farm and the Amana Colonies
concepts.contentHtml:
Brook Farm, at West Roxbury near Boston, was founded in 1841 by George Ripley, a former Unitarian minister, and his wife Sophia Ripley, as a joint-stock community where intellectual and manual work would be shared. It grew out of the Transcendentalist circle, though Ralph Waldo Emerson declined to join and Margaret Fuller only visited. Nathaniel Hawthorne invested and lived there in 1841, found farm labor left little energy for writing, resigned in 1842, and later drew on the experience for The Blithedale Romance (1852). The community's school was its best source of income. In 1844 Brook Farm reorganized on the plan of the French socialist Charles Fourier and began a large central building, the Phalanstery. On March 3, 1846, the uninsured building burned before completion, and the community closed in 1847 in debt.

The Amana Colonies lasted far longer. Their founders belonged to the Community of True Inspiration, a Pietist movement begun in Germany in 1714 by Eberhard Ludwig Gruber and Johann Friedrich Rock, who believed God still spoke through inspired "instruments" (Werkzeuge). Led by the instrument Christian Metz, the Inspirationists emigrated in the early 1840s to Ebenezer, near Buffalo, New York, and from 1855 moved to Iowa, where they built seven villages.

Communal life held until 1932. Strained by the Depression and by younger members' wishes, the members voted for the "Great Change," separating church and economy: the Amana Church Society kept the worship, while a for-profit company, the Amana Society, Inc., took over the farms and workshops and issued shares. The Amana appliance brand began there in the 1930s and later became an independent company.

title: They Shall Take Up Serpents
description: Hensley, Mark 16, state bans, deaths of pastors and a reality show

concepts.title: Hensley and the Signs Following
concepts.contentHtml:
Religious serpent handling grew out of the Holiness and Pentecostal revivals of the early twentieth century in southern Appalachia. Its proof text is the ending of Mark's Gospel in the King James Version: "And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues; They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover" (Mark 16:17 to 18). Handlers read it as command and promise: taking up serpents is one of the "signs following" true believers, and they handle only when they feel "anointed" by the Holy Spirit.

The man usually credited with starting the practice is George Went Hensley (c. 1880 to 1955), an East Tennessee preacher who by his own later accounts began handling rattlesnakes in services around 1910. He gave different dates in different interviews, and the scholars Ralph Hood and W. Paul Williamson argue that handling arose independently in several places. Hensley was licensed as a minister in the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) in 1915 and left it in 1922; the denomination later disowned the practice. He preached across the Southeast and died in July 1955 near Altha, Florida, after a bite during a service, having refused medical treatment.

Scholars add a complication. Mark 16:9 to 20, the "longer ending," is missing from the two oldest complete manuscripts of Mark, the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and most textual critics regard it as a later addition. It remains in the King James Bible that handling congregations use, and most churches still treat it as canonical.

concepts.title: The Law Steps In
concepts.contentHtml:
Deaths and public alarm soon brought legislation. Kentucky passed the first state ban in 1940, forbidding the handling or display of snakes in connection with any religious service, after a Harlan County man complained that his wife had taken up handling at a church in Pineville. Georgia followed in 1941 with a law under which handling that led to a death could be punished by execution; juries were reluctant to convict, and the law was repealed in 1968. Tennessee and Virginia passed bans in 1947, North Carolina in 1949 and Alabama in 1950. Hensley himself was arrested more than once. West Virginia never passed a ban, and handling remains legal there.

State courts have consistently upheld these laws as health and safety measures, from Kentucky's Lawson v. Commonwealth (1942) to the leading case, Swann v. Pack (1975). In that case the Tennessee Supreme Court upheld an injunction against a Cocke County congregation and extended it to drinking strychnine, declaring that "Tennessee has the right to guard against the unnecessary creation of widows and orphans." The court drew the line courts usually draw in such cases: belief is protected absolutely, but conduct that endangers life can be restrained. No snake-handling case has reached the US Supreme Court.

Enforcement has always been patchy, and many congregations simply carried on. Today some states act mainly through wildlife laws: Tennessee, for example, forbids keeping dangerous venomous snakes without a permit. Membership is unknown because handlers are private and their churches independent. Scholarly and press estimates run from about 1,000 to 5,000 people in perhaps 40 to 125 small congregations, mostly in Appalachia.

concepts.title: Deaths, Faith and the Cameras
concepts.contentHtml:
Most handlers are not bitten at a given service, but over a lifetime bites are common and some are fatal. Counting is hard because many deaths were reported only in local papers. In Them That Believe (2008), Hood and Williamson listed 89 documented deaths from snakebite and nine from drinking poison, with the earliest documented bite death reported in 1919. Other writers give totals of 100 or more. All such figures are minimum counts. Believers who die after refusing treatment are not, to their congregations, proof that the faith is false; many say that the person's time had come, or that he or she had handled without the anointing.

Pastors are among the dead. Mack Ray Wolford died of a timber rattlesnake bite in West Virginia in 1983. His son, Pastor Mark Randall "Mack" Wolford, a well-known defender of the practice, was bitten during an outdoor service in May 2012 and died that night, aged 44, after delaying treatment.

In 2013 the National Geographic Channel aired Snake Salvation, a 16-episode reality series following two pastors: Jamie Coots of Middlesboro, Kentucky, and Andrew Hamblin of LaFollette, Tennessee. Late that year Tennessee wildlife officers seized dozens of snakes from Hamblin's church; in January 2014 a grand jury declined to indict him, though the snakes were not returned. On February 15, 2014, Coots, 42, was bitten on the hand during a service, turned away paramedics, and died at home that night. The series was not renewed, and his son Cody succeeded him as pastor.

title: Why America Made New Religions
description: Disestablishment, the religious marketplace thesis, Christian Science and the Millerites' heirs

concepts.title: Disestablishment and the Religious Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
Most colonies had an established church supported by taxes: the Church of England in Virginia and the South, Congregational churches in most of New England. The Revolution broke the system up. Virginia passed Thomas Jefferson's Statute for Religious Freedom in 1786, and the First Amendment (1791) barred Congress from making any law "respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." It bound only the federal government, so states could keep their own establishments: Connecticut disestablished in 1818, New Hampshire in 1819, and Massachusetts, the last, in 1833.

Without state support, churches had to win members. The sociologists Roger Finke and Rodney Stark, in The Churching of America (1992), argued that disestablishment created a free religious economy of competing "firms." By their estimates only about 17 percent of Americans were church adherents in 1776, about 34 percent by 1850, and more than half by the early twentieth century. The winners were "upstart" sects with zealous, poorly paid preachers and demanding standards: Methodists, by their count, rose from about 2.5 percent of adherents in 1776 to about 34 percent in 1850.

Critics reply that colonial church membership was harder to obtain than later adherence, so low colonial figures may understate religious involvement. Jon Butler's Awash in a Sea of Faith (1990) describes a gradual Christianization of a population steeped in folk magic; Nathan Hatch's The Democratization of American Christianity (1989) stresses populist, anti-elite culture. Reviewing the studies, Mark Chaves and Philip Gorski (2001) found no consistent evidence that pluralism raises participation, and David Voas and colleagues (2002) argued that many positive findings were statistical artifacts. Few dispute that disestablishment made founding a new church unusually easy.

concepts.title: Christian Science: Mind over Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
Mary Baker Eddy (1821 to 1910), born in Bow, New Hampshire, suffered years of chronic illness. From 1862 she was treated by, and studied with, Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, a mental healer in Portland, Maine. In February 1866, weeks after Quimby's death, she fell on ice in Lynn, Massachusetts. She later said she recovered after reading an account of one of Jesus's healings, and she dated her discovery of Christian Science to that moment. A local newspaper reported her injury as serious, but her doctor later denied ever saying her case was hopeless, and the episode remains disputed.

Her book Science and Health appeared in 1875, later expanded as Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures. It teaches that God, wholly good and wholly spirit, is the only reality, so that matter, sin, sickness and death are errors of mortal mind, to be healed by prayer that corrects false belief. Eddy founded the Church of Christ, Scientist, in Boston in 1879, reorganized it around The Mother Church in 1892, and in 1908, at 87, launched The Christian Science Monitor, a respected daily newspaper.

How much Eddy owed Quimby has been argued since the 1880s. Critics called her a plagiarist; biographers as different as Gillian Gill and Caroline Fraser grant his strong influence but not plagiarism. Graver controversy surrounds children of Christian Scientists who died of treatable illnesses without medical care; parents were prosecuted for manslaughter or neglect in cases from the 1880s to the 1990s, with mixed outcomes. The 1936 religious census counted about 269,000 American Christian Scientists, near the peak. Eddy's Church Manual forbids publishing membership figures, so later numbers are outside estimates, all pointing to steep decline.

concepts.title: After the Great Disappointment
concepts.contentHtml:
The Millerites followed William Miller, a Baptist lay preacher from Low Hampton, New York, who calculated from the Book of Daniel that Christ would return about 1843; the movement finally fixed on October 22, 1844. When nothing visible happened, the Great Disappointment scattered them. Some returned to their old churches, some abandoned faith, and some even joined the Shakers. (The movement and its failed date are covered in the topic The Apocalypse Didn't Come.)

The most durable heir grew from a reinterpretation. Hiram Edson and others concluded that the date had been right but the event misunderstood: on October 22, 1844, Christ had entered the inner room of a heavenly sanctuary to begin a final judgment, as they read Daniel 8:14. Joseph Bates persuaded the group to keep the seventh-day Sabbath, Saturday, and Ellen G. White's visions guided it. The Seventh-day Adventist Church formally organized at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1863. It preached a health message of vegetarianism and abstinence, ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium where John Harvey Kellogg and his brother developed corn flakes, and now reports more than 24 million baptized members, most of them outside North America.

Adventist ideas shaped another movement too. As a young man in Pittsburgh, Charles Taze Russell was drawn back to Bible study around 1870 by an Adventist preacher, Jonas Wendell, and from 1876 worked with the Adventist writer Nelson Barbour before they split. Russell began publishing Zion's Watch Tower in 1879. Those of his Bible Students who stayed with the Watch Tower Society under Joseph Rutherford took the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931. Smaller heirs include the Advent Christian Church.
